The fear
CHAPTER 2
$ git rebase -i HEAD~3
$ git push --force
fatal: ...what did I just do?!

One wrong command and I'd break something — so the risky parts, I left to a developer. I was collaborating on the build, not driving it.

Then it clicked
CHAPTER 3
Then I actually drove it — branch, commit, resolve, ship. The same save points and shared cloud I already knew, just owned end to end. That was the whole leap?!

The whole thing was 6 steps and 4 words. The gap was never knowledge — it was doing it myself. So — let me walk you through the same six.

You are here

Here's everything I wish someone had told me that day — in about 20 minutes, with zero fear and zero jargon.

01
The reframe

Git is just save points for your work.

🎮

Like a video game

Every commit is a checkpoint you can always return to. Made a mess? Jump back to an earlier one.

⏪

Undo for real life

It's a time machine for a whole project — not one file, but every file, with a note on why it changed.

🛟

Nothing gets clobbered

Once you commit, that snapshot stays put — safe, labelled, and yours to return to.

Why it exists

It kills final_final_v3_REALLY_final

Without Git 😖

  • ✕
    design_final_v2_FINAL.fig
  • ✕
    "Which version is the real one?"
  • ✕
    Two people overwrite each other's work
  • ✕
    No idea who changed what, or why

With Git 😌

  • ✓
    One source of truth, always current
  • ✓
    Every change is labelled: who, what, why
  • ✓
    Everyone works at once, nobody clobbers
  • ✓
    Roll back to any point in seconds
The one thing people mix up

Git ≠ GitHub

Git

The save-point machine

Lives on your laptop. It's the tool that takes the snapshots. Works even with no internet.

📷 Think: the camera.

GitHub

The shared cloud

Where the save points live online so a team can share them — and where you review & discuss changes.

☁️ Think: the shared photo album (a Google Drive for code).

The whole vocabulary

The only 4 words you actually need

repo

Repo

A project folder that Git is watching. "The repo" = the project.

commit

Commit

One save point + a short note on what changed and why.

branch

Branch

A parallel version of the project to work on, without touching everyone else's — you flip between them in place.

pull request

PR

"Here's my change — please look, then merge it in." Where review happens.

The #1 mix-up

A branch is not a folder

What people picture 😖

  • ✕
    "It makes a new folder somewhere on my computer."
  • ✕
    "I have to go find it and copy my files in."
  • ✕
    "My other work disappears when I switch."

What actually happens 😌

  • ✓
    Same folder, same files — Git just swaps what's inside them
  • ✓
    Switching a branch rewrites the files in place
  • ✓
    Your other branch is safe, waiting — nothing is lost

A branch is a parallel timeline, not a place on disk. One project folder — many save-lines you flip between.

You’ll do thisck-ux-concepts will spin up 5 UX concepts from one spec — parallel lines of work, one starting point. Think of it like branching.
Where the talking happens

A PR is a conversation

💬

Comment on the change

Feedback lands on the exact line that changed — not lost in a Slack thread or an email.

🔁

Reply with a commit

Someone asks for a tweak? Push another commit — the same PR updates. The whole thread stays in one place.

✅

Approve → merge

Once everyone's happy, merge. Your branch folds into the shared version.

You already live in comment threads — Docs, Figma, Slides. A PR is the same thing, just attached to the actual change instead of floating next to it.

02
Why this matters · if you're a designer

Your design decisions get a history

  • 1
    Your tokens, copy & assets live with the product — versioned, never lost in a Slack thread.
  • 2
    See exactly what changed — text you own (tokens, copy) shows up as a diff: a highlighted before/after. Changed images show side-by-side.
  • 3
    Every change carries a who & why — the reasoning travels with the design, not lost in DMs.
  • 4
    Tweak a color token or a button label yourself — no ticket, no waiting.

The real unlock

You stop watching the build from the outside —
and start participating in it.

You speak the same language as the people shipping your product. That changes every conversation you have with them.

03
Do it with your hands

The everyday loop — 6 steps, every time

1

Sync

Pull the latest main (the shared version everyone builds on)

2

Branch

Start your own safe line of work

3

Edit

Do your thing — design, copy, docs

4

Commit

Save a snapshot + a note

5

Push

Send your branch to the cloud

6

PR

Propose it → review → merge

That's the everyday Git loop developers run — the wrapper around the real building. Six steps. You'll do it yourself in a minute. (You only clone once, on day one — after that, it's just this loop.)

A habit that saves you

One branch, one thing

🎯

One piece of work

A single feature, fix, or artifact per branch — not a pile of unrelated changes stacked together.

☁️

Open a draft PR early

Cut the branch, open a draft PR right away, then keep committing to it. Your work is backed up in the cloud from the first commit — never stuck only on your laptop.

🔀

Merge, then start fresh

Open the PR, get it merged, then cut a new small branch for the next thing.

Already deep on one giant branch? 😅 The way out: open a PR now, merge what's ready, then cut small branches from here. A short branch is easy to review — a giant one scares everyone, including you.

You’ll do thisLike this: ck-ux-full-design designs only the flows your feature touches, nothing unrelated — the design side of “one branch, one thing.”
The monster that isn't

A merge conflict is just… two people, one line

<<<<<<< your branch Alex was here! ======= Sam was here! >>>>>>> main

Git isn't broken. Two people edited the same line, and Git is politely asking a human to pick.

  • 1
    Delete the <<< === >>> markers
  • 2
    Keep the text you want (often: keep both)
  • 3
    Save, then stage & commit to finish the merge — done. That's the whole "monster."
You’ll do this/ck-utility-sync pulls the latest, merges main into your work, and walks you through exactly this — the same command from the loop.
Deep breath

"Help, I think I messed up"

🧽

Undo file edits

Before committing — throw away changes to a file.

git restore <file>

↩️

Undo last commit

Take back the commit but keep your actual work.

git reset --soft HEAD~1

🧭

When in doubt

Run git status — your best friend — then ask a teammate. No shame.

Golden rule: your commits are snapshots. Committed work is very hard to truly lose. That's why we commit early and often.

Keep this open

The 90% you'll actually use

I want to…Command
Copy the repo downgit clone <url>
Start my own line of workgit checkout -b my-branch
See what I changedgit status
Stage my changesgit add .
Save a snapshotgit commit -m "message"
Send it to GitHubgit push -u origin my-branch
Get everyone else's changesgit pull

A handful of commands cover almost everything you'll ever do. Print it, bookmark it — no memorising required.

You don't need to become a developer.
You just need to stop being afraid.

The whole thing is 6 steps and 4 words — and now it's yours. Not a passenger anymore; you're in it.
